key_concept: For a complete cycle $\Delta U = 0$, so by the first law the net heat supplied equals the net work done, which is the area enclosed by the cycle on the $p$-$V$ diagram.
steps: The gas returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$. The first law $Q = \Delta U + W$ then gives $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}}$.
The work done in the cycle equals the area of the rectangle $abcd$: $W = (V_b - V_a)(p_a - p_d)$.
The cycle runs clockwise ($a \to b \to c \to d$), so the net work is done by the gas and is positive: $W = +600\ \text{J}$.
Therefore the total (net) heat supplied is $Q = W = 600\ \text{J}$.
why_not_others: 400 J and 500 J come from misreading the rectangle's sides. 800 J results from wrongly using $p = 300 + 100$ or similar. Only the enclosed area $3 \times 200 = 600$ J is the net heat.
common_trap: Students often add only the heat absorbed in the steps $d \to a$ and $a \to b$, which gives $600 + 2250 = 2850$ J, instead of the net heat over the cycle, or they treat the cycle as anticlockwise and change the sign.
time_saving_tip: For any closed cycle, the net heat equals the enclosed area on the $p$-$V$ graph. Just multiply the rectangle's sides ($\Delta V \times \Delta p$), and the 'monatomic' detail is not needed.
